tier1.text: Each adrenal gland makes hormones, substances carried by the blood, that help the body cope with stress and control blood pressure. The gland sits near the top of a kidney, with an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The cortex makes aldosterone, a hormone that helps the body keep sodium and fluid and raises blood pressure. In short-term stress, the medulla sends out its main hormone, epinephrine, which is also known as adrenaline.

tier2.text: Each adrenal gland helps control the stress response, blood pressure, blood volume and water balance by making hormones, substances that travel in the blood to act on cells in other parts of the body. Each gland is a wedge of tissue attached to the top of a kidney by a fibrous capsule. Inside, the gland has an outer cortex made of glandular tissue and an inner medulla made of nervous tissue. The cortex is made of layers: the outer zona glomerulosa makes hormones such as aldosterone; the next, the zona fasciculata, makes hormones such as cortisol; and the inner zona reticularis makes androgens, a class of sex hormones. Aldosterone makes the body hold on to sodium and fluid, raising blood volume and blood pressure. Cortisol raises the blood level of glucose, the simple sugar that cells use for energy. The cortex releases cortisol and related hormones during long-term stress, whereas the medulla responds to sudden, short-term stress. The medulla is made of large, irregularly shaped nerve cells called chromaffin cells, which make epinephrine, also called adrenaline, and norepinephrine. Epinephrine and norepinephrine speed up the heart and raise blood pressure, readying the body to fight a threat or run from it. The hypothalamus, a part of the brain, controls both parts of the gland in different ways: the cortex through adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), a pituitary hormone, and the medulla through nerve impulses.

quotes.quote: As noted earlier, the adrenal cortex releases glucocorticoids in response to long-term stress such as severe illness. In contrast, the adrenal medulla releases its hormones in response to acute, short-term stress mediated by the sympathetic nervous system (SNS).
quotes.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

sentences.text: The medulla is made of large, irregularly shaped nerve cells called chromaffin cells, which make epinephrine, also called adrenaline, and norepinephrine.

quotes.quote: The medullary tissue is composed of unique postganglionic SNS neurons called chromaffin cells, which are large and irregularly shaped, and produce the neurotransmitters epinephrine (also called adrenaline) and norepinephrine (or noradrenaline).
quotes.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

sentences.text: Epinephrine and norepinephrine speed up the heart and raise blood pressure, readying the body to fight a threat or run from it.

quotes.quote: These hormones increase the heart rate, pulse, and blood pressure to prepare the body to fight the perceived threat or flee from it.
quotes.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

sentences.text: The hypothalamus, a part of the brain, controls both parts of the gland in different ways: the cortex through adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), a pituitary hormone, and the medulla through nerve impulses.

quotes.quote: The hypothalamus of the brain influences both portions of the adrenal gland but by different mechanisms. The adrenal cortex is regulated by negative feedback involving the hypothalamus and adrenocorticotropic hormone; the medulla is regulated by nerve impulses from the hypothalamus.
quotes.citation: SEER Training Modules: Adrenal Gland. U.S. National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute.

quotes.quote: adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH): anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete corticosteroid hormones (also called corticotropin)
quotes.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.
